entries.title: Klopp wins first game as Germany coach, without 'top dogs'
entries.summary: It may have taken a little longer than he would have liked, but Jürgen Klopp has finally won a game as Germany coach. Despite a number of debutants, it was a familiar face who stood out in the victory over Serbia.
entries.content:
Germany

Klopp wins first game as Germany coach, without 'top dogs'

October 2, 2026

It may have taken a little longer than he would have liked, but Jürgen Klopp has finally won a game as Germany coach. Despite a number of debutants, it was a familiar face who stood out in the victory over Serbia.

After 47 days, three matches and 44 squad players, Jürgen Klopp has a first win as coach of Germany's men's fotball team. A straightforward 2-0 victory over Serbia in the Nations League on Thursday meant the former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach avoided becoming the first Germany boss to win any of his first three games.

"I'm really happy today," Klopp told German public broadcaster ZDF. "We were outstanding when defending and when we had the ball. We simply played wonderful football."

Klopp had raised a few eyebrows by naming two squads for the four fixtures in this extended international window. But after a somewhat fortunate draw against the Netherlands and a shock loss to Greece with the more senior of the squads, it was left to those lower down the pecking order to get things going Thursday in Munich.

Bischof gets first goal on home turf

That meant a completely new starting XI and debuts to ‌goalkeeper Jonas Urbig ⁠and ⁠winger Derry Scherhant. Such players should "develop without the top dogs" Klopp said before the game. And while Urbig was untroubled by Serbia, his Bayern Munich teammate Tom Bischof made his mark by turning in the opener after Florian Wirtz, one of the sprinkling of senior players, hit the post. It was Bischof's first goal for Germany in only his second national team game.

"It's indescribable," said Bischof after the game at Bayern's Allianz Arena. "The stadium was on fire. I let it all out and was overjoyed." Unfortunately, he said, "my knees hurt a little from sliding on my knees. But that doesn't matter."

After a string of tournament failures, the latest new dawn for Germany comes with a little more patience. As well as Klopp's track record, there is a general acceptance from inside the country and abroad that Germany are no longer a top tier side.

"We're not the Bayern Munich of European football," Klopp said prematch. "We're a team that needs to find its footing."

Klopp: 'I liked everything'

While one win against a limited Serbia side will not change that, the emphatic nature of the performance impressed the new boss.

"I liked everything — the opening phase, the middle section, and the end. Our counter-pressing was off the charts," said the man whose Gegenpressing (Counter-pressing) tactic became his trademark at Dortmund. "We can afford to take all the liberties and risks we want when we win the ball back together. Everyone was there during our pressing moments."

The second half brought more debuts for players who may not have made a traditional 26-man squad. Cologne winger Said El Mala and Brentford's Vitaly Janelt made their Germany bows while Celtic's Mika Baur became the country's 1,000th men's international.

It was "surreal," Baur said. "Today was a highlight for everyone, not just for me with my debut."

Wirtz provides spark and hope

While Klopp may have seen enough from a few of the second string to afford them opportunities in the future, the performance of Liverpool midfielder Wirtz, who scored Germany's second goal, may be the most critical of the night.

Wirtz, 23, has struggled to find his best form in the Premier League and has blown hot and cold in his 47 caps for Germany. A cool and composed finish suggested that the player who was so highly regarded at Bayer Leverkusen can be coaxed to life by Klopp.

"It was loads of fun. Every single one of us gave it our all on the field. We stuck to the game plan and did almost everything right," said Wirtz, who took the captain's armband later in the game. "The players around me made it easy for me. We had a lot of movement in the middle. We were all fired up."

The challenge now for Klopp is to work out which of his wide pool of players are the ones he can rely on to take Germany to Euro 2028 and beyond. The next step is a chance for revenge against Greece in Thessaloniki on Sunday.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: UK police make another arrest in RAF Fairford case
entries.summary: Counter terrorism police said a dual UK-Iranian national was arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. Five men arrested on Sunday remain on bail.
entries.content:
October 1, 2026

Counter terrorism police said a dual UK-Iranian national was arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. Five men arrested on Sunday remain on bail.

Police in the United Kingdom on Thursday said that another man had been arrested as part of the investigation into Sunday's security incident at a US-run air base in Gloucestershire.

The arrest of the dual UK-Iranian national came after British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC there were "strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford."

Iran's embassy in London earlier said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation it was involved while Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Burnham was "barking up the wrong tree."

What police have said

Counter terrorism police said that a 27-year-old dual UK-Iranian national was arrested in London "on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006."

They said that a second man who is a UK national was also questioned under caution and that searches of two properties had taken place.

"The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry," said Counter Terrorism Policing's Vicki Evans.

"As we've made clear, we're looking at all possible angles — including possible foreign state involvement. I'd like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation," Evans said.

Sunday's events at RAF Fairford

Five men in their 20s, all from the London area and with British citizenship, were arrested on Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran.

They were wearing face coverings.

Police seized three "suspicious" white vans and evacuated around 85 households in the vicinity, bringing in bomb disposal teams.

Police said a quantity of petrol was but no explosive devices were found in the vans.

The suspects have since been released on bail in a move questioned by US President Donald Trump.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Ethiopia and Eritrea sever ties amid Tigray fighting
entries.summary: Ethiopia said it was expelling Eritrean diplomats in response to Eritrea's "direct and indirect acts of hostility." Eritrea said it had "no choice but to reciprocate in kind."
entries.content:
Ethiopia

Ethiopia and Eritrea sever ties amid Tigray fighting

October 1, 2026

Ethiopia said it was expelling Eritrean diplomats in response to Eritrea's "direct and indirect acts of hostility." Eritrea said it had "no choice but to reciprocate in kind."

Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties on Thursday after Ethiopia accused its northern neighbor of involvement in renewed fighting in the Tigray region.

The Ethiopian Foreign Ministry was the first to announce that it was shutting its embassy in Eritrea "in response to Eritrea's direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence against Ethiopia."

The Ethiopian embassy ​in Eritrea had been reopened in 2018 as ​part of ⁠the rapprochement that culminated in Prime ⁠Minister ​Abiy Ahmed receiving the Nobel Peace Prize.

Ethiopia's Foreign Ministry also declared ten Eritrean diplomats "persona non grata", accusing them of "involvement in activities that pose a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security." The Eritrean diplomats were given 48 hours to leave the country.

Hours later, Eritrea's Foreign Ministry called the move "absurd" and said the expulsion of ten of its diplomats from Addis Ababa had effectively shuttered its embassy there.

Eritrea said it therefore had "no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia with all the negative corollaries ​that this entails."

Reports of earlier blast at Ethiopian military headquarters

The measures came following reports of an explosion overnight at Ethiopian military headquarters in Addis Ababa.

The AFP news agency reported that the explosion took place at the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) headquarters between midnight and 1:00am local time, citing diplomatic and security sources with the information.

The sources could not provide further information relating to the nature of the blast or who was responsible, or if there had been any casualties.

The Associated Press, citing security sources, reported that there had been three blasts that came after the government banned the use of drones in the capital.

It's not clear whether the blasts were related to any attack or whether they had been part of training exercises.

Eritrea has denied allegations that it supports an armed alliance — which includes the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the the Amhara Fano National Movement, and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) — currently fighting Ethiopian government forces. The coalition is named Alliance for Survival.

Hundreds have been killed and wounded since last week's resumption of heavy fighting in northern Ethiopia.

Clashes have been ongoing and have have taken place along several fronts.

The United Nations has called for de-escalation of the fighting and for talks between the government and the recently formed alliance.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: After 2 years in office, how has Claudia Sheinbaum changed Mexico?
entries.summary: Two years after taking office as Mexico's first female president, Claudia Sheinbaum can take credit for a lower homicide rate and improved social benefits. But violence and corruption persist.
entries.content:
Mexico

After 2 years, Sheinbaum's Mexico sees incremental change

October 1, 2026

Two years after taking office as Mexico's first female president, Claudia Sheinbaum can take credit for a lower homicide rate and improved social benefits. But violence and corruption persist.

Since Claudia Sheinbaum first took office in 2024 as Mexico's first female president, she has largely adhered to the political agenda of her mentor and predecessor, Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador.

But she has also had to contend with several problems that go far beyond Mexico's borders: violence inflicted by drug cartels, tens of thousands of missing persons and the growing political pressure from US President Donald Trump.

Fewer murders — but more missing persons

Sheinbaum has been able to report some progress when it comes to the security situation in Mexico. In her second government report, presented in September, she touted a 51% drop in the daily homicide rate since 2024.

To what extent this progress can be attributed to Sheinbaum's administration is, however, a matter of debate. While the Mexican Institute of Human Rights and Democracy has also noted progress in the effort to reduce homicides, the Mexico Evalua think tank has said there isn't enough statistical evidence to attribute the decline directly to measures taken by Sheinbaum.

And other indicators highlight a problematic trend. Mexico Evalua, referring to the government's own figures, pointed out that the number of recorded cases of kidnapping and enforced disappearances has surged by 127% over the last decade, "crimes against life" by 197% and femicide by 53%.

As of June 2026, the national register recorded a total of 135,271 missing persons. At the start of Sheinbaum's time in office in October 2024, that figure stood at around 115,000, according to an analysis by Red Lupa, a citizen-led network dedicated to monitoring disappearances.

"There is a lack of political will [to address the issue]," said Edgar Cortez, a project coordinator at the Mexican Institute of Human Rights and Democracy in Mexico City. On the one hand, he said, the government sees little political benefit, while at the same time it's lacking the technical expertise to coordinate the varied measures implemented at the state and federal levels.

Displacement — another consequence of violence — is also disrupting the lives of millions across the country. According to the National Institute of Statistics and Geography, violence or crime forced at least one member in 510,000 households — some 1.6 million people — to change their place of residence between October 2020 and October 2025.

Selective crackdown on corruption

Eduardo Bohorquez, director of civil society organization Transparencia Mexicana, told DW he has noted a shift in the government's strategy when it comes to fighting corruption. Two years on, he said the government is now focusing on the links between federal employees and organized crime.

As example he gave Operacion Enjambre, during which more than 100 public officials of varying political affiliation were arrested — including mayors, former mayors and police commanders, according to Mexico's security chief Omar Garcia Harfuch.

Critics, however, have accused the government of taking a selective approach. To date, no incumbent or former governor of Sheinbaum's ruling Morena party has been either prosecuted or detained for corruption or alleged links to organized crime.

Shienbaum has announced a package of reforms to tackle corruption, and Bohorquez said that will show whether or not her administration will actually chart a different course than that of her predecessor.

Placating Trump a top priority

Domestic and foreign policy have been closely linked during Sheinbaum's two years in office. Most of that time has been shaped by Donald Trump's return to the White House in January 2025, and his administration's increasing pressure on drug cartels, migration and trade.

Trump has accused Mexico of not doing enough to tackle the cartels, with Washington classifying several Mexican criminal organizations as terrorist groups. The US president has repeatedly threatened to take unilateral action against the cartels. Sheinbaum, however, has opposed any US military actions on Mexican territory, calling instead for "cooperation without subordination."

At the same time, Mexico and the US have been cooperating closely — especially when it comes to migration. Between 2024 and 2025, the number of migrant contacts registered by US authorities along the US-Mexico border dropped by more than 84%, from 1.5 million to around 238,000.

Economic cooperation is also key to the cross-border relationship. Mexico and the US are currently negotiating several trade issues, including the future of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, known as USMCA. For its part, Mexico is hoping to reduce Trump's tariffs on steel, aluminum and automobiles.

After talks with Trump in September, Sheinbaum said both sides were working toward a trade deal. It remains a tricky balancing act for the Mexican president — developing the closest possible trading relationship with her country's most important economic partner, while at the same time not giving the impression that Mexico is giving up its political sovereignty under pressure from Washington.

Progress on social rights

The outlook is brighter when it comes to economic and social rights, with Cortez of the Mexican Institute of Human Rights and Democracy singling out the increase in minimum wage and government benefits for older people and those living with disabilities.

When it comes to other human rights concerns, however, he hasn't seen "any progress or setbacks." Alongside the staggering number of missing persons, Cortez also pointed out attacks on human rights defenders and journalists, along with a failure to sufficiently consult with Indigenous groups and rural communities when it came to major construction projects.

Sheinbaum has announced a plan to introduce a nationwide law against femicide that would align the various regulations on the local and state level, said Cortez. "That could end up being a positive, but the problem will be to put it into practice," he added.

Transparency without 'accountability'

The government's record on transparency remains problematic, according to observers, with Sheinbaum doing away with the National Institute for Transparency, Access to Information and Protection of Personal Data, or INAI. The responsibilities of the independent agency, which had been in place for two decades, have since been divided among several state entities.

"Instead of making things easier, everything has become fragmented," said Bohorquez of Transparencia Mexicana. Anyone looking for information from Congress, the judiciary, the military or local authorities now needs to go directly to the source.

Bohorquez also gave a mixed reaction to Sheinbaum's daily press conference, saying that while it was "a very effective political communication tool it didn't provide accountability."

For Cortez, that reflects a fundamental question of Sheinbaum's political priorities. New social programs bring "instant political benefits," he said, while advancing on civil and political rights required long-term effort and didn't allow the government to "immediately capitalize on political gains."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Ethiopia: Who could bring the warring sides to the negotiation table?
entries.summary: Ethiopia might be facing its most complex armed conflict in contempary times. The fragile 2022 peace deal has collapsed. International mediators have failed. How will the country manage to return to normal?
entries.content:
Ethiopia

Can anyone broker a new peace between Tigray and Ethiopia?

October 1, 2026

Ethiopia might be facing its most complex armed conflict in contempary times. The fragile 2022 peace deal has collapsed. International mediators have failed. How will the country manage to return to normal?

Just four years after a landmark peace deal officially halted the devastating Tigray war, fighting has escalated once again in northern Ethiopia in recent weeks. 

Just days before full-scale fighting resumed, several armed groups which had previously considered each enemies formally announced an alliance with a common goal: To bring down Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's federal government.

But this time, the lay of the land looks quite different from the previous conflict: Parties outside the country have been accused of meddling in the situation, with each having their own motives to want to destabilize Abiy's government.

This has raised fears about prolonged instability hitting the Horn of Africa.

Reasons for the collapse of the peace deal

The 2022 Pretoria Peace Agreement ended the conflict between the Ethiopian federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which cost hundreds of thousands of lives in the course of two years.

Negash Mohammed, a journalist with DW's Amharic department. believes that the deal collapsed for three key reasons — or rather because three key actors in the conflict were largely neglected at the negotiation table.

Mohammed explained that the ultimate agreement didn't factor in the role of Eritrea in the conflict, which had fought alongside Ethiopia against the TPLF; it ignored the part that Amhara militias — known as Fano — played in the war, who later felt sorely excluded from the negotiations; finally, it ignored harliners within the TPLF who viewed the peace peace as nothing but military defeat.

Tensions between the federal government and the Fano escalated further when Addis Ababa moved to forcibly disarm the militias instead of addressing their grievances.

"The federal government has its own shortcomings," said Mohammed. "Instead of convincing the other side, it went on to aggravate the grievances they [already] had."

An alliance of former enemies

Mohammed also emphasized the fact that this coalition against the federal government includes several groups which have otherwise little to do with each other.

It includes the Oromo Liberation Army, a faction of the Ogaden National Liberation Front as well as multiple smaller armed groups from the western Benishangul-Gumuz region — in addition to ethnic militant factions from Afar, which borders Tigray.

Eritrea meanwhile appears to have shifted sides in the current situation: While not officially a member of the alliance, the neighboring country is believed to be providing support to the rebels.

Patricia Rodrigues, a senior analyst at Control Risks, a global intelligence and security consultancy, referred to the level of strategic coordination among these various groups in the current conflict as "quite significant" and "definitely alarming for the federal government."

She noted, however, that cracks might eventually appear: "How long this coalition lasts, because all of them have very different interests and represent very different ethnic constituencies, remains to be seen," she told DW.

Rodrigues added that, based on Control Risks' assessment, the fighting is likely to remain limited to Ethiopia's northern regions, particularly those situated along the borders between Tigray, Amhara, and Afar.

Furthermore, she highlighted that the idea of it spreading across the entire country was rather unlikely due to the difficulty of nationwide coordination, taking into consideration the rough terrain of the nation and the fragmentation of other opposition groups.

Could the conflict have been prevented?

Rodrigues also pointed out the failure of sustained international engagement after the end of the crisis in 2022 as a key reason for the current conflict_

She noted that while the Pretoria agreement saw some early proof of implementation — including the TPLF's surrender of heavy weaponry in 2022 and 2023 — international attention had soon shifted to other global crises, leaving both sides free to quietly rearm and conscript supporters.

"It was more of a stopgap or a ceasefire, but people were quickly rearming in the background," she told DW.

Rodrigues also noted that the United States had recently lifted sanctions imposed during the 2020–2022 conflict — a step which, according to Mohammed, diminishes the West's leverage in the conflict to push combatants toward coming to the negotiation table.

The real cost of war

In the meantime, civilians are bearing the cost of the warring parties: People caught up in the crossfire have been fleeing the conflict once more, adding further to a population of internally displaced persons (IDPs) that has not recovered from the previous war.

"Since 2020, they have not returned to their areas. They are still in makeshift IDP centers," Mohammed said, adding that there have also been isolated reports of drone strikes hitting civilian areas and of rebel groups deploying military hardware inside schools and clinics.

Telephone and internet connections have also been cut in parts of Tigray and Amhara, electricity has been disrupted, and flights have been suspended to several cities including Kombolcha and Lalibela.

Despite official assurances from all parties that civilians would be protected, Mohammed says that the reality on the ground tells a different story: "Words and practice are very contradictory."

Limited prospects for mediation

Mohammed also noted that outgoing UN Secretary-General António Guterres dispatched a special envoy to the Horn of Africa, charged with mediating between the African Union, regional powers, and Egypt — many of the same parties involved in brokering the Pretoria agreement.

However according to Mohammed, meaningful negotiations are unlikely to bear fruit until at least one of the sides involved in the conflict "comes to understand that this violence will not help them to achieve what they want."

Rodrigues agrees, stressing that she cannot be optimistic about "an international or a regional mediation being the solution to the current fighting," adding that "intense, but geographically contained" fighting will continue for the foreseeable future.

Adapted from the AfricaLink Podcast by Silja Fröhlich

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

entries.title: Finland probes suspected break-ins at politicians' homes
entries.summary: The Finnish prime minister has not ruled out the possibility of foreign involvement in the suspected break-ins at the homes of members of parliament.
entries.content:
Finland

Finland probes suspected break-ins at politicians' homes

October 1, 2026

The Finnish prime minister has not ruled out the possibility of foreign involvement in the suspected break-ins at the homes of members of parliament.

Finnish police are investigating a series of suspected break-ins at the homes of members of parliament, officials announced on Thursday.

Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo was asked by a reporter if a foreign power could be behind the suspected intrusions, and he replied that it was "very possible... quite possible in these times."

"If someone tries to destabilize Finland, our sense of security, or our support for example for Ukraine, it has the opposite effect. It strengthens our unity," he added.

Meanwhile, Finnish President Alexander Stubb stated, "An attack against a member of parliament is an attack against democracy."

What do we know about break-ins?

After the media reported on the alleged intrusions, speaker of parliament Jussi Halla-aho confirmed that parliament had been made aware of a "significant" number of break-ins and attempted intrusions at the homes of several politicians.

"I cannot comment precisely on the number of suspected cases known to us, but in any event, it is significant," Halla-aho said at a press conference.

He added, however, that the known cases had occurred over a longer period of time, with the first believed to have taken place about a year ago.

Halla-aho also emphasized that, at this point, no information is available about the motive or the perpetrator.

Paula Risikko, the deputy speaker who leads the parliamentary security group, said she was informed of the suspicions last week.

She added that the Helsinki police had been tasked with the initial stage of the investigation.

MPs advised to keep an eye out

Earlier this week, newspaper Ilta-Sanomat reported that MPs had been warned of potential break-ins and that the newspaper was aware of at least two home intrusions.

All members of parliament were told to keep an eye out, report any suspicious activity, and file police reports if necessary.

Helsinki police confirmed that a preliminary inquiry had been opened. "The inquiry is at an early stage, and the police have nothing further to comment on at this time," it said.

Since the Kremlin began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Finland has been on high alert. The Nordic country, which shares a 1,340-kilometer (830-mile) border with Russia, abandoned its decades-long policy of military non-alignment and joined NATO in April 2023.

Finland previously accused Moscow of "hybrid warfare" and orchestrating a surge of migrants at their shared border in 2023. The Kremlin denied the allegations.

Edited by Zac Crellin

entries.title: Renee Good's family sues Trump admin over fatal ICE shooting
entries.summary: The family of Renee Good, one of two US citizens fatally shot by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis in January, has sued President Donald Trump's administration alleging negligence and civil rights violations.
entries.content:
United States of America

Renee Good's family sues Trump admin over fatal ICE shooting

October 1, 2026

The family of Renee Good, one of two US citizens fatally shot by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis in January, has sued President Donald Trump's administration alleging negligence and civil rights violations.

Relatives of Renee Good, the 37-year-old woman shot dead in her car in Minneapolis by a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent on January 7 this year, are suing the US government in a civil lawsuit connected to her death that was filed on Thursday. 

Good and her wife had been taking part in daily protests in the city against the deployment of armed and often masked federal agents deployed to Minnesota to arrest and identify undocumented migrants for deportation.

The lawsuit alleges "federal conspiracy with discriminatory design and authorized use of force against observers," saying that this resulted in "extreme and unconstitutional force" being exerted against "people exercising their rights under the [US] constitution's Bill of Rights."

Good's killing, followed two weeks later by the death of nurse Alex Pretti, intensified the already-sizeable protests against the deployment of ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents in Minneapolis known as Operation Metro Surge. 

What do the lawsuits allege?

The plaintiffs in the twin civil suits from the Romanucci Blandin Law firm, filed on October 1, are Good's brother Brent Ganger — acting as trustee for her other next of kin including her three children — and her partner Becca Good. 

One names the United States of America as the sole defendant.

The other names a series of responsible government and border control officials, including but not limited to the ICE officer who shot Good in her car, White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy Stephen Miller, and the US Secretary of Homeland Security at the time of the shooting, Kristi Noem.

"Renee's death was not an accident," Romanucci Blandin Law wrote in a statement. "It was the predictable result of a coordinated campaign by senior officials in this administration to target Minnesotans of Somali or Hispanic origin and silence anyone who dared to raise their voice in protest."

They allege that Operation Metro Surge "was built on exaggerated fraud accusations that the White House embraced as a pretext for thousands of masked, unidentified federal agents to rove neighborhoods and stop people based on how they looked."

It said that government officials "told agents to force confrontations with observers like Renee and led agents to believe that they would face no consequences for using force."

The crackdown in Minneapolis, which has a large Somali population, came as part of President Donald Trump's tough stance on migration and border security, and amid his assertions that local authorities in some Democrat-run states do an inadequate job fighting crime and irregular migration.

'She was pure love'

Becca Good, Renee's wife, made her public comments about the shooting at a press conference in Minneapolis on Thursday.

"I'm here today because last January the whole world had to watch as our entire universe was destroyed," she said.

Becca said of her wife: "She was pure love. She was ⁠funny. She ​was smart. She was gorgeous."

"Renee believed in something simple: that being good can change the world," she added. "She believed everyone deserves love ​and compassion, care and dignity, no matter who they were or where they came from."

Brett Ganger, Renee Good's brother, said, "The hole in my family and myself created by my sister’s passing is hauntingly apparent".

"What happened to Renee was completely senseless and the fact ​that there's been no accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy is completely mind-blowing," Ganger said.

"What happened to America? Something must change now," he stressed.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Germany expresses optimism over Montenegro's EU ambitions
entries.summary: Germany's top diplomat said Montenegro has made "remarkable progress" in the accession process. The small Balkan state is being seen as a frontrunner among six regional candidates.
entries.content:
Montenegro

Germany expresses optimism over Montenegro's EU ambitions

October 1, 2026

Germany's top diplomat said Montenegro has made "remarkable progress" in the accession process. The small Balkan state is being seen as a frontrunner among six regional candidates.

Germany on Thursday expressed optimism regarding Montenegro's bid to become part of the European Union.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that the Western Balkans country's ambition to join the bloc was being "heard in Brussels and in all European capitals."

Wadephul made the comments after traveling to Montenegro on Wednesday to attend the annual meeting of European foreign ministers as part of the so-called Berlin Process.

What did Wadephul say?

"Montenegro has made remarkable progress towards EU membership – it thus sets an example for the Western Balkans," Wadephul said in a post on X.

He posted up a picture of himself embracing Ibrahimovic and thanked him for hosting the Berlin Process Foreign Minister's meeting, adding that there had been agreement to "foster regional cooperation on reconciliation and reforms."

"Those who are willing and able to join the European Union and meet the criteria can succeed in the coming years," said Wadephul at the meeting with his Montenegrin counterpart Ervin Ibrahimovic.

EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos was also at the talks held in the coastal city of Budva.

EU candidate countries in the Western Balkans are Montenegro, Albania, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and North Macedonia. Kosovo is also a potential candidate for membership.

Montenegro's EU ambition not just a pipe dream

Of the six Western Balkan candidates, Montenegro is seen as the frontrunner, having been pursuing membership for 22 years.

The small, mountainous nation of 623,000 people adopted the euro as its de facto currency as early as 2002, declared independence from the union with Serbia in 2006, and joined NATO in 2017.

With public support for accession reportedly at around 80%, Montenegro is aiming to become the EU's 28th member state by 2028. 

Progress on economic and democratic reforms previously prompted the EU's enlargement commissioner to flag the possibility of completing technical negotiations by the end of the year, making the 2028 timeline appear realistic.

Among the other Western Balkan countries, Albania is also seen as a promising candidate, but Kosovo's path to EU membership remains the most complicated, with five EU member states still refusing to recognize its independence from Serbia.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: North and South Korea trade accusations over landmines that injured three soldiers
entries.summary: A mine blast that injured three South Korean soldiers has renewed scrutiny of North Korea's actions along the border and raised questions about its strategic goals.
entries.content:
North Korea

Is North Korea pushing the limits of the DMZ?

October 1, 2026

A mine blast that injured three South Korean soldiers has renewed scrutiny of North Korea's actions along the border and raised questions about its strategic goals.

Pyongyang and Seoul are trading increasingly hostile accusations across the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that divides the peninsula, 10 days after three South Korean soldiers were injured by a land mine on the South's side of the border.

The latest tensions may reflect a broader North Korean effort to test South Korea's resolve while extending its control to the outer limits of its territory, including an area that has effectively been a no-man's land for more than 70 years, according to a professor of foreign policy at South Korea's Kyung Hee University.

"The North revised its constitution in March this year and officially stated that they intend to define the absolute geographical limits of the nation, and that includes within the DMZ," said Choo.

"They want to maximize their territory and it is my sense that they would like to push the Military Demarcation Line [MDL] — the half-way point in the DMZ — further south," he told DW.

"I see the placing of landmines on the South's side of the line as a purely political act by the North, an attempt to threaten and intimidate the South."

Why Seoul blames North Korea

The three men were part of an 18-strong patrol clearing a new route through the DMZ as part of an investigation into the activities of North Korean troops in the western sector of the zone. The four-kilometer-wide strip of land has divided the peninsula since the Korean War ended in an armistice in 1953. 

Shortly before 11 a.m. on September 21, the patrol was around 10 meters south of the MDL when a staff sergeant detonated a mine. A second mine went off as the unit commander approached to provide assistance. Both men were successfully evacuated and have undergone surgery, with a third soldier treated for minor wounds.

The South Korean military has conducted an investigation with the United Nations Command, which administers the armistice on the border, and concluded in a report released this week that the mine was of North Korean origin.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff on Wednesday accused the North of sowing mines to the south of the MDL, a breach of the armistice agreement, and demanded an apology from Pyongyang and a commitment to halt the construction of further fortifications along the border.

"This constitutes a blatant violation of the Armistice Agreement and undermines the spirit of existing inter-Korean agreements and must be halted immediately," Kang Hyun-woo, chief director of operations, said in a press briefing.

"North Korea must immediately cease activities that heighten tensions on the Korean Peninsula, such as its so-called 'border fortification.' We strongly demand an apology and responsible measures from the North," Kang added.

In a statement, the UN Command said it had "determined that an Armistice Agreement violation occurred. UNC is addressing the violation through established Armistice mechanisms."

Many in the South are demanding more resolute action on the grounds that failure to respond will be taken as a sign of weakness in Seoul.

Na Kyung-won, a politician from the conservative opposition People Power Party (PPP), has demanded that the South Korean military carry out exercises simulating a "decapitation attack" against North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

She has also called for the restart of propaganda broadcasts from loudspeakers on the border and for dissident groups to be allowed to launch balloons carrying propaganda into the North.

A pattern of border confrontations

Yu Yong-weon, also of the PPP, told reporters on Wednesday that North Korean troops had crossed the MDL around 20 times in August and on 30 occasions in September. On each occasion, South Korean troops fired warning shots when the incursions were detected.

An editorial in the Korea JoongAng Daily on Thursday said North Korea must be "held accountable" for the incident, arguing that Pyongyang's denial of responsibility "demands a firm response, clear accountability and stronger border enforcement."

The North is not backing down, however, with Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, accusing the South of staging a provocation and threatening to retaliate. 

In a statement published by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on Wednesday, Kim Yo Jong dismissed the South's allegations as a "self-staged farce" and accused the "South Korean armed gangs" of using the incident to justify political and military provocations against Pyongyang.

Accident or calculated provocation?

Andrei Lankov, a professor of history and international relations at Seoul's Kookmin University, is more willing to view the landmine detonations as an accident.

"It makes no sense to me for North Korea to do this deliberately," he said. "At the moment, the North wants to keep a low profile and do nothing that could provoke the South. There is no gain in a deliberate attack like this."

Lankov believes a more likely scenario is that the mines were shifted from the northern side of the MDL in heavy rain or natural movements of the terrain, meaning that the North's protestations of innocence are genuine.

"I also do not think the South Korean government has any interest in escalating the situation further and that they will hope this is quickly forgotten," he said. "They will want to brush it under the carpet."

Choo, however, is less convinced and senses a growing anger in South Korean society that the government is not standing up to provocations from north of the border.

"I believe that resuming the propaganda broadcasts over the border would be an effective response, but I do not believe this government will do that," he said. "This government is trying very hard to connect with the North, but I see a failure to take a firm line this time being interpreted in the North as a sign of weakness in Seoul.

"Not responding would give Pyongyang a green light to push a little more and then a little more again," he said. "There is a lot of anger here that the government is not doing enough to protect soldiers who are serving on the DMZ, to protect the people and to protect our territory."
